issues.legal_issue: A tax paid on property used in a trade is deductible as a business expense when it is incidental to carrying on the trade, even if the taxpayer pays it in the capacity of both owner and trader.
material_facts: The non-resident shipping companies paid Japanese local taxes on business assets, including vessels and other tangible property.
The assets were used in the companies’ businesses during the relevant years.
The payment of the tax was incidental to carrying on the businesses.
issues.conclusion: The tax was deductible as a business expense under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(xv), expenditure incidental to the business and laid out for commercial purposes may be deducted. Travancore Titanium Product Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Kerala held that expenditure must have a direct and intimate connection with the business and be incurred in the taxpayer’s character as a trader. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal qualified that principle: where an owner-cum-trader pays an expense that is really incidental to carrying on the business, it is treated as incurred as a trader and is deductible.

predicates.business_income_deduction_case: The proceeding concerns whether a payment may be deducted in computing income from a business.
predicates.tax_paid_on_business_property: The taxpayer paid a tax in respect of property belonging to the taxpayer.
predicates.property_used_in_trade: The property was used by the taxpayer in carrying on the trade.
predicates.payment_incidental_to_trade: The payment was incidental to carrying on the taxpayer’s trade.

issues.definition: When a business-income deduction case concerns tax paid on property used in the trade and the payment is incidental to the trade, the tax is deductible as a business expense.

issues.legal_issue: A foreign local tax on specified property is not a tax of a similar character to a national tax on a person’s net wealth merely because both taxes concern assets.
material_facts: The Japanese tax was a local tax imposed by a city, town or village on specified categories of property located there.
The taxable property included land, houses and certain depreciable tangible assets, with specified exclusions.
The Japanese tax was calculated by reference to the value of the specified property at generally standard rates, subject to a maximum rate.
The Indian wealth tax was a national tax on the taxpayer’s net wealth, broadly determined by aggregating assets and deducting debts, and its rates increased with the amount of net wealth.
The assets subject to the Japanese tax were used in the companies’ businesses, and payment of the tax was incidental to carrying on those businesses.
issues.conclusion: The Japanese local property tax was not a wealth tax of a similar character within the meaning of the 1972 amendments, so those amendments did not bar its deduction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40(a)(iia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, as amended by the Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1972, and section 4 of that Amendment Act disallow wealth tax, including a foreign tax of a similar character. Whether a foreign tax is of a similar character depends on the taxes’ essential nature and structure, including what is taxed, how the taxable base is determined, and the character and rates of the tax. The Court distinguished a local tax on specified property from a national tax on net wealth. It also relied on Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal for the principle that a tax other than wealth tax on business assets remains governed by the ordinary business-expense deduction rule.
